body_markdown:
Popular though it may be in this day and age to stake out an opinion and ride it out till the bitter end, it turns out that people do, on occasion, change their minds. Chalk it up to advancing age or the chance to hop behind the wheel of something we’ve never driven or any number of other eye-opening factors; we’ve discovered that many of our “hot” takes on cars have changed over the years. And that’s usually for the better.


Here’s how a few of our stances have evolved. Let us know yours in the comments.


## Fast Isn’t Everything


[Chris Stark](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/chris-stark/)


That whole “when all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail” thing was definitely true for me as a young enthusiast. I only ever saw stuff in the context of how fast it was, and anything that wasn’t performance-oriented didn’t interest me.


Whether it’s age or having gone quickly for long enough, I’ve learned that there’s more to enjoy about cars than acceleration and lateral grip. It’s a simple observation, but it took a surprisingly long time to get here, and seeing this hobby through multiple lenses has opened up new worlds for me to appreciate. — *Eddy Eckart*


## Manuals Aren’t Everything


Flickr/SenseiAlan


Mine falls along the same lines as Eddy’s. I used to scoff at anything but a manual transmission. How dare you consider wheeling something that does part of the work for you? Have you ever heard of *driver involvement* , bro? Are you going to let technology and engineering ease the amount of work it takes just to commute? On the highway? In stop-and-go traffic every once in a while? Well, what about to the grocery store and back? That’s two ninety-degree corners and two miles of straight roads; you want an automatic transmission to shift for you there?


Yes, yes, I do actually. Listen up, younger me: We’re going to get soft. We’re going to get tired, and despite our best efforts, we’re going to drive pretty boring roads full of traffic for more than 70% of our time behind the wheel. An automatic is just fine, maybe even preferable. — *Nathan Petroelje*


## Prewar Cars: Not Just for the Silent Generation


Broad Arrow


I used to put basically everything built before World War II on the pay-no-mind list. I thought they were slow, drove like trucks, all pretty much looked the same, that kind of thing. Like with anything, though, once you really learn about the history and context behind something, the respect follows. Actually getting behind the wheel of a few cars from the ’20s and ’30s helps as well. So many of the design features and equipment from back then are fascinating; some of the coachbuilt stuff from the ’30s is completely unique, and driving a car from back then is a very special, very involved experience that’s different from anything else. — *Andrew Newton*


## Over-Modification


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Andrew is really on to something there, as I drove a Cord 810 in modern traffic and it blew my mind.


My choice for this question pertains to aftermarket speed or hot-rodding parts. High performance is great, but the roads around me are too horrible for most any suspension with tubular control arms jammed with Delrin or plastic bushings. The number of times I’ve had to work on vehicles that have been over-cammed or over-carb’d has traumatized me. And the shockingly poor quality of some aftermarket vendors (I won’t name names) aimed at the hot rod and restomod communities makes me question every switcheroo from OEM to an aftermarket part. I understand the appeal when starting from scratch in something basic like a Model A, but if you are pulling out a factory component for its aftermarket replacement in anything made in the last 60 years, it is absolutely a “buyer beware” affair. Well, at least for me! — *Sajeev Mehta*


## Beware of Altering a Car’s Character


Courtesy of Mecum Auctions


It is possible to take away too much of a car’s character.


For the longest time, I thought as long as a car cast roughly the same silhouette and still drove with pedals and a steering wheel, it was the same car. Now I’m at least not so sure. The line itself is unclear, but somewhere deep within a car is an unseen widget—its character—that is *so* easy to screw up with modification and can be hard to get back once you’ve crossed a certain line. Restoration or modification, the goal doesn’t change how fragile that little widget is. Years ago, I did not understand its existence, but now I at least have to admit it exists, has mysterious power, and will likely escape me forever. — *Kyle Smith*


## The Beetle


Cameron Neveu


The original, first-verse VW Beetle. Had one as my first car, and did not care for the handling, the wheezy little motor, for the scarcity of heat in the winter and the absence of air conditioning in the summer; even the fact that air from the spare tire powered the windshield washer seemed to annoy me. But while I didn’t exactly flip, I did grow to appreciate what VW did with the car, and kept doing beyond any imagined history. I still don’t particularly want one, but when I see one at a car show, in a parking lot or, rarely now, on the road, it makes me smile. — *Steven Cole Smith*
